stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Seedlings of the desert shrub Calvera are rare beneath mature Calvera plants, and ecologists long attributed this pattern to chemistry: the shrubs' roots, they argued, release compounds that keep seeds in the surrounding soil from germinating. In a recent study, however, ecologist Dana Okafor found that Calvera seeds sown in a greenhouse germinated at nearly identical rates in soil collected beneath shrubs and in soil taken from open ground, while seeds she placed beneath living shrubs in the field were mostly carried off by rodents within days. Okafor's results therefore cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: the shrubs' roots release chemical compounds into the soil that surrounds them.
rodents sheltering beneath the shrubs eat most of the seeds that fall there.
the soil beneath the shrubs contains substances that prevent seeds from germinating.
seedlings of the shrub are uncommon in the ground beneath mature shrubs.
explanation: The old view says something in the soil under the shrubs stops seeds from germinating. Okafor tested that directly: seeds germinated just as well in soil taken from under the shrubs as in open-ground soil. So the part of the old view her greenhouse result attacks is the claim that this soil holds germination-blocking substances. Notice that her study never checked whether the roots release compounds at all. It only checked whether the soil stops germination, so the doubt lands on that claim.

A.why: You saw that the old view is under attack and picked its first half. But Okafor never tested whether the roots release compounds. She tested whether the soil under the shrubs blocks germination. The roots could release plenty of compounds that simply don't affect seeds, so her results say nothing against this claim.

B.why: This sits on the wrong side of the 'however'. Okafor's field observation points toward rodents, so her results support this idea rather than doubt it. It also goes too far: the passage says the seeds were 'carried off', not eaten.

D.why: This is the observation that both explanations are trying to account for. Neither side disputes it, and the passage states it as fact. Okafor questions why seedlings are rare under the shrubs, not whether they are.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because recordings of the Brenna Valley dialect made in the 1960s capture the dropping of word-final t chiefly in speakers then under thirty, linguists long concluded that the feature was an innovation of that generation. Historian Ioan Maddock, however, has examined some 400 letters written by Brenna Valley farmers born in the 1850s and 1860s, many of whom spelled words such as "night" and "want" without a final t, a spelling absent from surviving letters by their own parents. Maddock's findings thus cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: Brenna Valley farmers born in the 1850s and 1860s dropped final t in their speech.
the dropping of final t in the dialect began with speakers who were young in the 1960s.
speakers under thirty in the 1960s dropped final t more often than older speakers did.
the spellings found in personal letters can reveal how the letters' writers actually spoke.
explanation: Separate the old conclusion from the evidence it rested on. The evidence was that 1960s recordings show t-dropping mostly in young speakers. The conclusion was that the feature began with that generation. Maddock's letters show the feature about seventy years earlier, among people born in the 1850s and 1860s. That attacks where the feature started, not what the recordings show. So the idea in doubt is that it began with speakers who were young in the 1960s.

A.why: This is what Maddock's letters suggest, so it sits on the wrong side of the 'however'. The blank needs the idea his findings weaken, not the new claim they support.

C.why: This is the trap that remains after you spot the old view. It restates the evidence the old view rested on, not the conclusion drawn from it. Maddock's letters say nothing about how often different age groups dropped t in the 1960s. The recordings still stand. What falls is the conclusion that the feature started with that generation.

D.why: This is an assumption Maddock's own argument depends on. His case only works if spelling reflects speech, so his findings can't cast doubt on it. It is also not the view the passage sets up to be challenged.
